Sources: Rockwood & Green's Fractures in Adults, 10th edition, Ch. 32 · AO Foundation Surgery Reference (Clavicle / Scapula modules)

Introduction

The clavicle suspends the shoulder girdle from the axial skeleton. Injury at either end — acromioclavicular or sternoclavicular — disrupts that suspensory function. AC injuries are far more common and usually benign; posterior SC dislocations are rare but can be true emergencies.

  • AC injuries predominate in males under 30 in contact sport, from a direct blow to the lateral shoulder.
  • SC injuries are usually benign, but posterior patterns threaten the trachea, oesophagus, great vessels and brachial plexus.
  • CT is the imaging modality of choice for the SC joint; plain radiography (Zanca + axillary) remains the workhorse for the AC joint.
  • Early and prompt reduction is indicated for posterior SC dislocations and posterior physeal injuries.
  • There remains no clear consensus on when AC operative management is essential, which prognostic signs predict nonoperative failure, or which procedure gives the best function with least morbidity.

Mechanism of injury

Acromioclavicular joint

  • Fall on an outstretched arm locked in extension drives the humeral head superiorly into the acromion — typically low-grade AC injury.
  • A medially directed force to the lateral shoulder drives the acromion into and beneath the distal clavicle — higher grades, more displacement.
  • Falling or being tackled onto the adducted lateral shoulder produces compressive (medial) and shear (vertical) force, tearing both AC and CC ligaments.

One common misconception is that the clavicle 'elevates' above the acromion. In reality the injury force drives the acromion medially and downward in a progressive pattern — AC ligaments, then CC ligaments, then the deltotrapezial fascia. Once suspensory support is lost, the scapula and arm droop inferiorly under gravity. The characteristic deformity is caused by inferior displacement of the shoulder, not elevation of the clavicle.

POPULATION
Males under 30
AC injuries predominate in contact sport, from a direct blow to the lateral shoulder.
FREQUENCY
AC 12% · SC 3%
Of 1,603 shoulder girdle injuries reviewed by Cave et al.; the SC joint is the least commonly dislocated major joint.
DIRECTION
Mostly anterior
Nettles & Linscheid: 57 anterior versus 3 posterior in 60 SC dislocations.
THE SEQUENCE
AC → CC → fascia
Failure runs in order; each step up the sequence raises the Rockwood grade.

Sternoclavicular joint

  • Direct force to the anteromedial clavicle pushes it posteriorly behind the sternum into the mediastinum (knee to the medial clavicle, seat belt, steering wheel, crush).
  • Indirect distraction: shoulder compressed and rolled forward → ipsilateral posterior dislocation; compressed and rolled backward → ipsilateral anterior dislocation.
  • Vehicular accidents are the most common cause, followed by sport. Most SC dislocations are anterior (Nettles & Linscheid: 57 anterior vs 3 posterior in 60 patients).
Bipolar and "floating clavicle" injuries

Injuries to both joints usually occur when one joint absorbs most of the trauma and the second sustains a low-grade injury with minimal displacement. Bilateral displaced injuries are termed bipolar injuries, "floating clavicle" or panclavicular dislocation. Reported cases describe anterior dislocation at the SC joint combined with posterior dislocation at the AC joint.

Sanders et al. reported six patients with dislocation of both ends of the clavicle: two lower-demand patients did well nonoperatively with only minor symptoms; the other four had persistent symptoms localised to the AC joint and underwent AC reconstruction, resulting in painless full range of motion and return to normal activity. These patterns typically occur with high-energy trauma and may be associated with neurologic symptoms. Bilateral (Balser) hook plates have recently been used with good success, but traditional open reduction with capsular repair and internal fixation augmentation has also been reported with success.

Associated injuries

Posterior SC dislocation — mediastinal injury

Significant concomitant mediastinal injuries must be considered to avoid catastrophic outcomes. These almost always occur with posterior SC fractures and dislocations.

StructureDetail
Tracheal compressionDisplaced medial clavicle can compress the trachea; acute airway compromise and subacute dyspnoea are key symptoms.
PneumothoraxPleural violation, especially in high-energy direct trauma.
Great vessel injuryDirect transection or compression; two recent reviews estimate incidence under 2%. Reports involve pulmonary artery, brachiocephalic vein, superior vena cava and innominate artery. Compression may present as thrombosis, including stroke-like symptoms from embolisation.
Oesophageal perforationRupture described, including a fatal tracheoesophageal fistula (Wasylenko & Busse).
Brachial plexus injuryMay occur with the injury pattern or from the static posterior clavicle position. Cervical spine injury must also be excluded — neurologic injury cannot be assumed to lie in the plexus.

Associated with AC injury

AssociationDetail
Glenohumeral intra-articular pathologyArthroscopy in grade III–V injuries: 18.2% SLAP lesions in a series of 77 patients; Pauly et al. found 15% (6/40) intra-articular pathology. No data support routine preoperative MR arthrogram or intervention unless a significant cuff tear is clinically suspected or symptoms persist.
FracturesDistal/lateral clavicle fracture is the most common. Coracoid base or neck fracture can leave CC ligaments attached to the fragment while presenting as a high-grade separation. Clavicle shaft fracture with AC separation is uncommon.
Coracoclavicular ossificationIntrinsic healing response after CC ligament injury; never associated with increased pain or dysfunction, but may need removal to allow full reduction.
Distal clavicle osteolysisFollows low-grade separations with an extended inflammatory response or repeated microtrauma. Bilateral changes should prompt consideration of rheumatoid arthritis, hyperparathyroidism or scleroderma; unilateral differential includes Gorham's massive osteolysis, gout and myeloma.
Scapulothoracic dissociationRare but devastating; lateral scapular displacement with traction injury to neurovascular structures. Consider in the unexaminable patient with a high-grade AC separation and lateral (not just superior) displacement. Mortality up to 10%, amputation risk 21%.
Brachial plexus abnormalitiesUncommon — Sturm and Perry identified only 2 AC separations among 59 brachial plexus injuries.

Clinical presentation and examination

Sternoclavicular joint

  • Posterior dislocation is usually more painful than anterior.
  • Anterior: prominent palpable medial clavicle. Posterior: normal anterior fullness of the chest is less prominent; the corner of the sternum is easily palpated.
  • Venous congestion in the neck or upper extremity in extreme cases.
  • Dry irritating cough, hoarseness, dysphonia, tight feeling in the throat.
  • Breathing difficulty, shortness of breath, choking sensation, dysphagia.
  • Decreased circulation to the arm — but present pulses do not exclude vessel injury.
  • Diminished sensation or weakness from brachial plexus compression.
  • Clinical findings cannot reliably differentiate anterior from posterior — confirm with CT in most cases.

Acromioclavicular joint

  • Expose the patient completely to compare with the uninjured shoulder.
  • Palpate the entire clavicular shaft to detect an associated shaft fracture.
  • Tenderness at the AC joint, the CC interspace and along the superior lateral clavicle.
  • Assess instability in both horizontal and vertical planes.
  • Shrug test — a type III (reducible) injury reduces with upward pressure under the elbow or active shrug; a type IV or V will not reduce if deltotrapezial fascia is interposed.
  • Viewing the seated patient from above shows the displaced clavicle translated posteriorly compared with the uninjured side.
  • Cross-arm adduction test — arm elevated 90°, elbow flexed ~90°, adducted across the chest; positive test produces pain specifically at the AC joint from compression across it.
  • O'Brien active compression test: 88% (55/62) of patients with AC pain had joint abnormalities at surgery or radiographic evidence of AC injury.

Imaging and other diagnostic studies

Ask the radiographer for the "AC joint", not the "shoulder". Good AC films need only one-third to one-half the beam penetration of the glenohumeral joint — routine shoulder technique overpenetrates, and small fractures are overlooked.

Zanca view
Bilateral, 10–15° cephalad, half penetration. No weights.
AC · PLANE TWO
Axillary lateral
Mandatory. Reveals type IV posterior displacement and missed coracoid fractures.
SC · SCREEN
Serendipity view
Anterior projects above the line; posterior below it.
SC · DEFINITIVE
CT, both sides
Distinguishes joint injury from medial clavicle fracture.
ViewTechniqueWhy it matters
Zanca view
AC joint		Beam tilted 10–15° cephalad, using one-third to one-half the penetration of a routine shoulder film. Bilateral AC joints on one cassette.On a routine AP the distal clavicle and acromion are superimposed on the scapular spine and subtle fractures are missed. The cephalic tilt projects an unobscured joint and standardises the clavicle–coracoid distance, which increases on a truer AP from parallax and bone contour.
Routine AP

AC joint		Supine, arm elevated over the head with the palm behind the head; humerus parallel to the longitudinal body axis, elbow pointing at the ceiling.Puts the coracoid in profile — the best view for a coracoid process fracture. SC joint		Include both sides with the patient supine and neutral.Distinguishes joint injury from medial clavicle fracture and defines minor subluxations. Caution: Tuscano et al. found >10% of 104 healthy subjects show substantial SC asymmetry that may be misread as pathologic.

Outcome measures and return to play

  • A recent validated patient-reported outcome score — the Nottingham clavicle score — has been developed to quantify residual dysfunction following SC and AC joint injury.
  • Traditional treatment of all injury patterns involves an early period of rest, ice and immobilisation with a sling.
  • Return to contact sport is variable, but recent reports suggest 10–15 days for low-grade type I or II AC injuries may be considered — though return to pain-free play takes longer.
  • Among Australian Rules football and rugby players, local anaesthetic injections for painful AC dislocations have been very successful with limited side effects; AC dislocations had the highest need at a mean of 5.7 games.
  • Chronic posterior SC dislocations and acute irreducible posterior dislocations require open surgery — this is an area of consensus, as the sequelae of posterior intrusion on the mediastinum must be avoided.

Acromioclavicular joint

The AC joint is a diarthrodial joint between the medial acromion and lateral clavicle, containing a fibrocartilaginous disc of varying size and shape.

StructureDetail
Joint inclinationAlmost vertical, or inclined downward and medially with the clavicle overriding the acromion by up to 50°. An underriding type also occurs. Approximately 50% of the time the clavicular articular surface overrides the acromial surface, producing incongruent surfaces.
Intra-articular discTwo types — complete and partial (meniscoid). Varies greatly in size and shape; with age the meniscus degenerates until essentially non-functional beyond the fourth decade.
InnervationBranches of the axillary, suprascapular and lateral pectoral nerves. The lateral pectoral nerve also supplies sensation to the anterior shoulder and glenohumeral joint, which explains diffuse pain referral. Gerber et al. found AC irritation produces pain over the AC joint, anterolateral neck and anterolateral deltoid.
AC ligamentsAnterior, posterior, superior and inferior. The superior AC ligament is the strongest; its fibres blend with deltoid and trapezius attachments, adding stability. Insertion lies 5.2–7 mm from the lateral clavicle in women, ~8 mm in men — resection medial to the capsular insertion causes horizontal instability.
Trapezoid ligament0.8–2.5 cm long and 0.8–2.5 cm wide. Arises from the coracoid anterior and lateral to the conoid, just posterior to the pectoralis minor tendon, extending superiorly to a rough line on the clavicular undersurface. May lie as little as 10 mm from the lateral clavicle.
Conoid ligament0.7–2.5 cm long, 0.4–0.95 cm wide. The more medial of the two; cone-shaped with its apex on the posteromedial base of the coracoid and base on the conoid tubercle at the apex of the posterior clavicular curve.

Biomechanics

  • Horizontal (AP) stability is controlled primarily by the AC ligament and capsule.
  • Vertical (superoinferior) stability is controlled primarily by the CC ligaments — the prime suspensory ligament of the upper extremity.
  • Fukuda et al.: at small displacements the AC ligaments are the primary restraint to both posterior (89%) and superior (68%) translation.
  • At large displacements the conoid provides the primary restraint to superior translation (62%), while the AC ligaments remain the primary restraint to posterior translation (90%).
  • At both large and small displacements the trapezoid is the primary restraint to AC joint compression.
  • The trapezoid has a greater role resisting posterior displacement of the clavicle; the conoid a greater role in anterior displacement.
  • Distal clavicle resection of only 5 mm avoids posterior abutment while preserving capsule and ligaments; larger resections cause excessive posterior translation.
  • Motion: the clavicle rotates 40–50° with shoulder elevation, but Rockwood et al. showed only 5–8° of rotation relative to the acromion — the rest is synchronous scapuloclavicular motion.

Horizontal (AP) stability = AC ligaments and capsule. Vertical stability = CC ligaments. The CC ligament also couples glenohumeral abduction and flexion to scapular rotation on the thorax — as the clavicle rotates upward it dictates scapulothoracic rotation through the conoid and trapezoid attachments.

Sternoclavicular joint

The SC joint is a diarthrodial saddle-type joint and the only true articulation between the upper extremity and the axial skeleton. The clavicular articular surface is much larger than the sternal, both covered with hyaline cartilage, and the surfaces are not congruent — so stability comes almost entirely from the surrounding ligaments.

Surgical danger zone

A “curtain” of muscles — sternohyoid, sternothyroid and scaleni — lies posterior to the SC joint and inner third of the clavicle, blocking the view of everything behind it. In most cases SC procedures are done with a cardiothoracic surgeon available.

  • Innominate artery
  • Innominate vein
  • Vagus nerve
  • Phrenic nerve
  • Internal jugular vein
  • Trachea
  • Oesophagus
  • Arch of the aorta
  • Superior vena cava
  • Right pulmonary artery
SPENCER ET AL.
Posterior capsule
The most important structure preventing BOTH anterior and posterior translation.
BEARN
Capsular ligament
The most important structure preventing upward displacement of the medial clavicle.
MOTION
30–35° elevation
35° combined forward and backward; 45–50° rotation about the long axis.
PHYSIS
Closes 23–25 yr
Last physis in the body to fuse; union may be delayed to age 31.
LigamentDetail
Intra-articular disc ligamentDense fibrous structure arising from the synchondral junction of the first rib and sternum, passing through the joint and dividing it into two spaces. Upper attachment on the superior and posterior medial clavicle. Acts as a checkrein against medial displacement of the inner clavicle.
Costoclavicular (rhomboid) ligamentShort and strong, with anterior and posterior fasciculi and an interposed bursa. Average length 1.3 cm, maximum width 1.9 cm, average thickness 1.3 cm. Anterior fibres resist excessive upward rotation and lateral displacement; posterior fibres resist excessive downward rotation and medial displacement.
Interclavicular ligamentConnects the superomedial aspects of both clavicles with the capsular ligaments and upper sternum. Prevents superior displacement of the clavicle with shoulder adduction and depression; failure force >53.7 N/cm² (Tubbs et al.).
Capsular ligamentCovers the anterosuperior and posterior joint, attaching primarily onto the medial clavicular epiphysis. Bearn showed it is the most important structure preventing upward displacement of the medial clavicle — division of the capsular ligament alone produced downward depression of the distal clavicle.

Biomechanics and motion

  • Spencer et al.: the posterior SC joint capsule is the most important structure preventing both anterior and posterior translation; the anterior capsule is an important secondary stabiliser.
  • The costoclavicular and interclavicular ligaments have little effect on anterior or posterior translation.
  • Range of motion: 30–35° upward elevation, 35° combined forward and backward movement, 45–50° rotation about the long axis.
  • In 2.5% of patients a small facet on the inferior medial clavicle articulates with the first rib (Cave).

The medial clavicular physis

FIRST TO OSSIFY
5th intrauterine week
The clavicle is the first long bone in the body to begin ossifying.
LAST TO APPEAR
Ossifies at 18–20 yr
The medial epiphysis is the last epiphysis in the body to appear.
LAST TO CLOSE
Fuses at 23–25 yr
Webb and Suchey found complete union may not be present until age 31.
CONSEQUENCE
Many are physeal
Boesmueller et al. found up to 16% medial physeal involvement in SC dislocation — so-called dislocations in young adults are often physeal injuries.

Rockwood classification explorer

Select a type to see the ligament status, clinical picture, radiographic criteria and the authors’ preferred treatment side by side. Rockwood expanded the original 1963 Tossy classification; grading is by the anatomic severity sustained by the AC ligaments, the CC ligaments and the supporting deltotrapezial musculature.

Type I
AC ligament sprain
Mild force to the point of the shoulder
Ligament status
AC ligaments strained but intact. CC ligaments intact. Deltotrapezial fascia intact.
Clinical
Joint remains stable. Minimal deformity, focal tenderness.
Radiographic findings
Radiographs normal except mild soft tissue swelling. No widening, no separation, no deformity.
Author’s preferred treatment
Nonoperative. Sling 1–2 weeks or until comfortable; icing; WBAT. PT for periscapular reactivation. Return to contact sports in 1–3 weeks.
Type II
AC ligaments ruptured
Moderate force to the point of the shoulder
Ligament status
AC ligaments ruptured. CC ligaments damaged but intact. Deltotrapezial fascia intact.
Clinical
Distal clavicle unstable in the horizontal (AP) plane; vertical stability preserved by the intact CC ligament. Slight relative upward displacement from CC stretching.
Radiographic findings
Subtle — partial (<50% clavicle width) superior subluxation vs contralateral on bilateral Zanca view. AC joint may appear widened from slight medial scapular rotation and posterior clavicular displacement. CC space equal to the normal side.
Author’s preferred treatment
Nonoperative. Sling typically 2–3 weeks but may be removed as soon as comfortable; icing, WBAT. PT for periscapular reactivation and rotator cuff strength training.
Type III
Complete AC dislocation
Severe force to the point of the shoulder
Ligament status
AC and CC ligaments both torn. Deltotrapezial fascia intact (reducible).
Clinical
Joint totally displaced; lateral clavicle completely above the superior acromial border. Reduces with upward pressure under the elbow (positive shrug test).
Radiographic findings
CC interspace 25–100% greater than the normal shoulder. Fractures may involve the distal clavicle or acromion.
Author’s preferred treatment
Immediate sling immobilisation; icing, NWB for 2–3 weeks; PT for gentle ROM. Continue nonoperative treatment for 3–6 months. If symptoms persist, consider MRI to assess for glenohumeral pathology; if persistent symptoms and no glenohumeral pathology at 9–12 months, consider chronic reconstruction. Exception: overhead athlete, manual overhead labourer, polytrauma, or strong patient preference → consider acute hook plate fixation.
Type IV
Posterior displacement
Force drives the scapula anteriorly and inferiorly
Ligament status
AC and CC ligaments disrupted; clavicle displaced posteriorly into or through trapezius.
Clinical
Relatively rare. Posterior displacement may be severe enough to tent the posterior skin; often irreducible.
Radiographic findings
Best seen on the axillary view — distal clavicle posterior to the glenoid and posterior to the end of the acromion. CC interspace may also be increased. CT of both shoulders helps in thick or polytraumatised patients.
Author’s preferred treatment
Operative treatment with acute hook plate fixation if the patient is young and active.
Type V
Severe type III variant
Larger force; muscle attachments also disrupted
Ligament status
AC ligaments, CC ligaments and deltotrapezial muscle attachments stripped — the distal clavicle lies subcutaneously.
Clinical
Marked disfiguration with severe downward droop of the extremity. Distal clavicle 'buttonholes' through the deltotrapezial fascia and is irreducible.
Radiographic findings
CC distance increased 100–300% (>100% vs normal side). The injured clavicle actually sits at approximately the same level as the normal side — the scapula is displaced inferiorly.
Author’s preferred treatment
Operative treatment with acute hook plate fixation if the patient is young and active.
Type VI
Inferior dislocation
Severe hyperabduction and external rotation with scapular retraction
Ligament status
AC ligaments disrupted in both subtypes. CC ligament intact in subacromial type, completely disrupted in subcoracoid type.
Clinical
Exceedingly rare; result of severe trauma, frequently with multiple other injuries. Distal clavicle occupies a subacromial or subcoracoid position.
Radiographic findings
Subacromial: CC distance decreased vs normal side. Subcoracoid: reversed CC distance with clavicle inferior to the coracoid. Be alert to intrathoracic injuries and associated clavicle and rib fractures.
Author’s preferred treatment
Rare and may relate to shoulder distraction injury — check neurovascular status. May be best treated with surgical reduction and AC complex repair/reconstruction.

How to grade correctly

PointDetail
OriginRockwood et al. developed the most widely accepted system, based on the original work of Tossy et al. (1963). Its strength is that it grades injury by the anatomic severity sustained by the capsular (AC) ligaments, the extracapsular (CC) ligaments and the supporting musculature — and therefore guides treatment.
How to measureUse bilateral Zanca views without weights. Measure (1) displacement of the distal clavicle above the acromion, as a percentage of clavicle width or in millimetres, and (2) the distance from the clavicular undersurface to the superior cortex of the coracoid.
Weighted stress viewsTraditionally used to differentiate type III from type V. This has never been validated against intraoperative findings. The authors' opinion: weighted-stress views do not increase diagnostic sensitivity, change the grade, or affect treatment — and are very painful acutely. Routine use is not recommended.
Normal variantsAC joint space normally diminishes with age; 0.5 mm in a patient over 60 is conceivably normal. Greater than 7 mm in men or 6 mm in women is pathologic (Petersson & Redlund-Johnell, 151 normal individuals).
Type III variantComplete AC separation with a normal CC distance should raise suspicion of a coracoid process fracture with intact CC ligaments attached to the fragment. The Stryker notch view is the ideal projection. Most are treated nonoperatively; if the fracture extends intra-articularly into the glenoid with ≥5 mm displacement, ORIF is considered.
Paediatric equivalentIn children and adolescents the distal clavicular physis lies medial to the AC capsular reflection. Injuries are often Salter–Harris type II fractures through the physis rather than true AC dislocations — the CC ligaments remain attached to the intact periosteal sleeve while the medial fragment displaces through a dorsal periosteal rent.

Sternoclavicular classification

Two methods: the anatomic position of the injury, and the aetiology of the problem. The OTA classification is based on the direction of dislocation, not aetiology.

CategoryDetail
Anatomic — anteriorMost common. The medial clavicle is displaced anteriorly or anterosuperiorly to the anterior margin of the sternum.
Anatomic — posteriorUncommon. The medial clavicle is displaced posteriorly or posterosuperiorly with respect to the posterior margin of the sternum. The OTA classification is based on direction of dislocation, not aetiology.
Sprain / subluxationLigaments remain intact and the joint is stable, though radiographic subluxation may be present. Capsular, intra-articular disc and costoclavicular ligaments may be partially disrupted.
DislocationCapsular and intra-articular ligaments are ruptured. If an acute traumatic dislocation does not heal, mild to moderate forces may produce recurrent dislocation — this is rare.
Physeal injuryMost SC separations in childhood and adolescence are physeal fractures with clavicular displacement, not true dislocations. Anterior or posterior. Frequently missed at first presentation.
AtraumaticSpontaneous subluxation or dislocation, typically in women in the late teens or young adult life with generalised ligamentous laxity. Usually self-limited with decreasing symptoms over time — operative treatment is not indicated.
Subacute / chronicInjuries presenting 7–10 days after injury are categorised as subacute, because closed reduction is unlikely to succeed and successful closed reduction after 48 hours is rarely reported. After 7–10 days, scarring and adhesions increase the risk of vascular injury with attempted reduction.
Other SC conditions to consider in the differential
ConditionDetail
InfectionConsider especially with IV drug use, immunocompromise, or indwelling subclavian catheters.
SC hyperostosisInflammatory condition of the SC joint and medial ribs with new bone formation and even ankylosis. Associated with Japanese ethnicity and palmoplantar dermatologic lesions.
Condensing osteitisWomen of late childbearing age; painful joint with sclerosis on radiographs.
Friedrich diseaseOsteonecrosis of the medial clavicle.
OsteoarthritisPostmenopausal; can appear as an anterior pseudosubluxation.

AC joint — nonoperative treatment

Indications
  • Type I AC joint injury
  • Type II AC joint injury
  • Type III AC joint injury
Relative contraindications
  • Chronic symptomatic injury
  • Failed nonoperative management
  • Athlete
  • Polytrauma
  • Heavy labourer

The principle

A simple sling is the currently favoured immobilisation device. The principle is to support the weight of the upper extremity and reduce stress on the injured ligaments. The goal of acute phase management is pain control.

Rehabilitation timeline — the authors’ approach

Day 0–7
Sling placed to fully support and elevate the arm. Icing. Weight bearing as tolerated.
Week 1
Shoulder range of motion begun for low-grade injuries.
Week 2
Formal physiotherapy for higher grades — shoulder and periscapular strengthening.
Week 2–4
Heavy stress and lifting once full ROM and no pain on joint palpation.
Week 4–6
Contact sport resumes, dictated by absence of pain with activity.

What to tell the patient

LOW-GRADE OUTCOME
Typically pain free by 2–3 weeks
But Mouhsine et al. found 52% of type I and II still symptomatic at an average of 6 years.
IF PAIN PERSISTS
Look for a cause
Post-traumatic arthritis, distal clavicle osteolysis, recurrent AP subluxation, trapped capsular ligament, loose cartilage, detached meniscus or an intra-articular fragment.
EARLY RETURN
Does not worsen the separation
No study has demonstrated progression of AC separation with early return to sport, though pain with collision sport is certainly a limitation.
THE TRIAL PERIOD
6 weeks before surgery
Unless neurologic or skin issues dictate earlier intervention.

No high-quality prospective study has demonstrated surgical benefit for type III injuries. Acute types I, II and III can be safely managed with 6 weeks of supervised rehabilitation, and still have excellent results with delayed reconstruction if this fails.

The evidence — randomised trials and long-term follow-up
StudyFinding
COTS (2015)Randomised type III–V injuries to anatomic reduction with hook plate vs sling and shoulder support for 4 weeks. Both groups began resistance exercise at 6 weeks; plates removed at a mean of 8.2 months. The nonoperative group had superior outcome scores at 6 weeks, 3 months and 6 months and returned to work earlier. Level I.
ACORN — Murray et al. (2018)Open reduction with tunnelled suspensory device (TightRope) vs sling for 3 weeks with identical rehabilitation. Nonoperative patients had significantly better scores at 6 weeks, with no functional difference at 1 year. Five patients failed nonoperative treatment and crossed over. Level I.
Joukainen et al. (18–20 yr)Longest follow-up of type III and V injuries. No significant difference in functional outcomes between operative and nonoperative groups, although the nonoperative group had more prominent and wider AC joints. Level III.
Verstift et al. (2021)Type I and II at 7–10 years: no significant functional impairment or arthritis versus the uninjured side. Deformity, osteolysis and ligament ossification were more common radiographically but did not affect outcome. Level III.
Historical pendulumConservative in the 1930s–40s; operative in the 1950s–70s (1974 poll: 60% temporary AC fixation, 35% CC fixation); back to nonoperative by the 1990s after RCTs of CC screw and K-wire fixation showed limited benefit and slower rehabilitation.

AC joint — operative treatment

Who gets an operation

CLEAR INDICATION
Types IV, V and VI
In active healthy patients — significant morbidity from a persistently dislocated, unstable AC joint with altered scapular kinematics.
AFTER A TRIAL
Failed type III
Persistent pain or inability to return to sport or work after 3–6 months. Delayed stabilisation still allows return.
CONSIDER EARLY
Overhead athlete
Selected young active patients in overhead activities, to avoid altered shoulder biomechanics.
CONSIDER EARLY
Polytrauma
Gallay et al. found worse shoulder function on both disease-specific and general health outcomes.

If operative treatment is chosen acutely, the authors recommend open reduction and hook plate fixation.

Variants with a coracoid fracture

USUALLY
Treat as a type III
Provided the deltotrapezial fascia is not largely disrupted and coracoid displacement is not severe.
IF INTRA-ARTICULAR
Consider ORIF
When the fracture extends into the glenoid, the authors use 5 mm or more of glenoid displacement as the criterion. CT is performed to evaluate this.

Evolution of technique

TechniqueDetail
Transarticular pin/wire fixationOne of the first techniques described, intended as temporary reduction while native soft tissue healed. Abandoned after reports of fixation failure, loss of reduction and disastrous hardware migration.
Bosworth screw (1941)Extra-articular transient 'screw suspension' for acute reducible dislocations, intended to allow CC ligament healing. The contrast between rigid fixation and intrinsic clavicle–scapula motion led to hardware failure, migration and coracoid fractures.
CC suspensionDacron grafts, wires and various sutures — a less rigid construct intended to hold the CC distance reduced while allowing motion and ligament healing.
Weaver–Dunn (1972) and modificationsDistal clavicle resection with transfer of the coracoacromial ligament to the distal clavicle. Still widely used but biomechanically inferior: ultimate load to failure 39% less than controls, with recurrent instability reported in up to 30%, typically AP at the AC joint. Good to excellent results historically in 75%.
Hook plateReported since the 1980s with good to excellent results; modified over time to lower profile and anatomic contour. Holds the clavicle reduced by hooking under the acromion and elevating the glenohumeral joint. The authors' preferred technique for selected acute type III and most type IV and V injuries. Requires planned removal — 6 months for acute fixation, 9–12 months when used for chronic reconstruction. Patients must know two operations are usually required.
Arthroscopic / arthroscopic-assistedWolf and Pennington first described all-arthroscopic AC reconstruction; Lafosse et al. described all-arthroscopic CC reconstruction transferring the coracoacromial ligament. Suture devices with cortical buttons for CC fixation, augmentable with graft and separate AC capsule repair. Meta-analysis found no difference between open and arthroscopic reconstruction in complications, loss of reduction or revision.
Anatomic CC ligament reconstruction (ACCR)Reconstructs both CC ligaments with a tendon graft fixed in two clavicle tunnels at the anatomic conoid and trapezoid insertions, with the remaining graft limb reconstructing the AC ligaments. The authors' preferred technique for chronic symptomatic injury, with adjunctive hook plate fixation.

Chronic AC injuries

  • Type I and II may develop late degenerative changes, though not at a rate different from the unaffected shoulder. Treat with NSAIDs, activity avoidance and intra-articular corticosteroid — most resolve.
  • If conservative care fails, distal clavicle excision (open or arthroscopic) can relieve pain. Preserve or repair the AC joint capsule to maintain AP stability, and limit resection to less than 10 mm.
  • Chronic pain and instability after complete dislocations (III, IV, V) should not be treated with isolated distal clavicle excision — this merely shortens the clavicle without stabilising it and is often associated with persistent or worsening symptoms. Excision must be combined with stabilisation.
  • A systematic review of ligament transfer vs non-biologic fixation vs biologic graft found no significant difference in complications, but superior functional scores with a biologic graft.

Author’s preferred treatment — AC dislocations

SC joint — nonoperative treatment

Most SC injuries can be managed non-invasively: most acute and chronic anterior subluxations and dislocations, acute traumatic posterior subluxations and some dislocations, and acute traumatic anterior and posterior physeal injuries of the medial clavicle.

Sprain or subluxation

FIRST 12 HOURS
Ice
Then heat for the following 24–48 hours.
REDUCTION
Draw the shoulders back
As if reducing a clavicle fracture. A sling and swathe supports the shoulder and prevents arm motion.
PROTECTION
4–6 weeks
Before release to contact sport or heavy activity.
ANTERIOR DISLOCATION
Try closed reduction
Consensus now favours initial closed reduction, with open reduction reserved for failure in acute traumatic dislocations.

Chronic anterior dislocation

Rarely requires reconstruction — most patients have few symptoms, nearly full range of motion, and can perform manual labour. Surgery is recommended only in extreme situations, for persistent instability symptoms or post-traumatic arthritis pain. AO Surgery Reference likewise treats anterior, superior and inferior dislocations as non-life-threatening, with expectant management and reassurance.

Posterior SC dislocation — the emergency

Acute posterior SC dislocation can be life-threatening if severely displaced or if an evolving haematoma affects breathing. Per AO Surgery Reference, immediate closed reduction in the operating room should be undertaken as a potential life-saving procedure.

WITHIN 48 HOURS
Reduce closed
Most posterior dislocations reduce closed inside this window, and most acute reductions are stable.
1–2 WEEKS
Scar forms
Tissues scar to the posterior clavicle; risk of vascular injury on reduction rises. Get a CT angiogram.
SKELETALLY IMMATURE
Often physeal
Lafosse: closed reduction succeeded in 0 of 4 posterior physeal separations — open reduction recommended.
CHRONIC
Operate
Late thrombosis, arterial occlusion and thoracic outlet syndrome are all reported in untreated posterior dislocation.

Before you reduce

EXCLUDE
Mediastinal injury
Careful examination for injury to the trachea, oesophagus, brachial plexus, great vessels and lungs.
IMAGE
CT of both medial clavicles
Add arteriography of the great vessels whenever vascular injury is suspected.
STAFF
Cardiothoracic cover
If a thoracic surgeon is available they should be present from the very beginning of the procedure.

The reduction window

0–48 hours
Most posterior dislocations reduce closed, and most acute reductions are stable.
7–10 days
Classified subacute — closed reduction unlikely to succeed, though success has been reported at 10 days.
1–2 weeks
Tissues scar to the posterior clavicle; risk of vascular injury on reduction rises. CT angiogram, vascular and bypass teams ready.
Beyond
Open reduction ± stabilisation, per Algorithm 32-2.

Closed reduction of posterior SC dislocation

R&G 10e — abduction traction, Buckerfield–Castle and towel-clip techniques
Step 1 of 5
Set up and time the attempt
Most posterior SC dislocations reduce closed if attempted within 48 hours of injury. Position supine with the entire arm prepped. Per AO Surgery Reference this is done under general anaesthesia in the operating room as a potential life-saving procedure, with a thoracic surgeon present from the beginning if available.
Step 2 of 5
Abduction traction technique
Place a 3- to 4-inch sandbag between the shoulders with the injured shoulder near the table edge. Apply lateral traction to the abducted arm, then gradually bring it back into extension. Countertraction may be applied to the chest wall. The clavicle usually reduces with an audible pop or snap, visible and palpable, and is usually stable. Beware: too much extension can bind the anterior surface of the dislocated medial clavicle on the back of the manubrium.
Step 3 of 5
Adduction traction (Buckerfield–Castle)
Supine with a 3- to 4-inch bolster between the shoulders. Apply traction to the arm in adduction while exerting downward pressure on the shoulder. The clavicle is levered over the first rib into position. Buckerfield and Castle reported success in seven patients in whom the abduction traction technique had failed.
Step 4 of 5
Direct reduction with towel clip
If traction fails, an assistant grasps or pushes down on the clavicle to dislodge it from behind the sternum. In a thick-chested patient or with extensive swelling, prepare the skin and use a sterile towel clip percutaneously. The clip must encircle the shaft of the clavicle — dense cortical bone prevents purchase into it. Combined arm traction plus anterior lifting force on the clip usually reduces the dislocation. A percutaneous Schanz pin or screw allows more forceful manipulation.
Step 5 of 5
Confirm and immobilise
Place the clamp and confirm position under fluoroscopy before applying traction, to protect against errant clamp placement and soft tissue injury. Reduction is typically audible and confirmed on fluoroscopy. Assess stability — gross instability with recurrent posterior dislocation should be addressed with additional procedures. Following reduction the joint is usually stable; treat with a sling for approximately 2–4 weeks.

Chronic SC dislocation and physeal injury

Why chronic posterior dislocation is not benign

STANKLER
Subclavian vein thrombosis
Reported at 4.5 years after the injury.
MEHTA ET AL.
Subclavian artery occlusion
Delayed occlusion at 6 months.
EGE ET AL.
Vascular compression
Bilateral, demonstrated on CT angiography at 2 years.
ALSO REPORTED
Thoracic outlet syndrome
With respiratory compromise and dyspnoea on exertion in unreduced dislocation.

Operative treatment is strongly recommended for skeletally mature patients with posterior SC dislocation.

Posterior physeal injuries

  • Posterior physeal injuries should be reduced when they present acutely, using techniques identical to SC dislocation. If stable reduction is achieved, hold the shoulders back in a figure-of-eight dressing or strap for 3–4 weeks.
  • Lafosse (30 patients): closed reduction succeeded in 50% (5/10) of posterior dislocations but 0% (0/4) of posterior physeal separations — closed reduction is hampered by the metaphyseal spike of the Salter–Harris II fracture line. Open reduction is recommended for posterior physeal separations.
  • The singular difference from adult dislocation: if a posterior physeal separation cannot be closed reduced and the patient is asymptomatic, the displacement can in theory be observed — the fracture usually unites and remodels, with potential extending to age 23–25.
  • Emms et al. reported subclavian thrombosis 2 years after an injury treated nonoperatively, precipitated by a second injury. Close observation for the first 2 years with serial vascular studies and/or CT is an important element of nonoperative care in the skeletally immature.

Author’s preferred treatment — traumatic posterior SC dislocation

AO — superior approach to the clavicle

Can be used for all lateral, medial and diaphyseal clavicle fractures. Plates for lateral clavicular fractures are typically placed superiorly; plates for diaphyseal or medial fractures can be placed anteriorly or superiorly.

Applied anatomy

SHAPE
S-shaped, three cross-sections
Flat laterally, tubular in the middle, prismatic medially. The flat-to-tubular junction is a stress riser — hence midshaft fractures.
DANGER
Medial/middle third junction
Subclavian artery and vein and the brachial plexus pass between the first rib and clavicle here, and are vulnerable to instrumentation.
PROTECTION
Subclavius muscle and fascia
Shield the neurovascular structures from the fracture in the middle third — but still exercise care with sharp instruments.
DEFORMITY
The SCM is not the culprit
The medial third stays put; the lateral two-thirds and shoulder girdle drop under gravity. Pushing the shoulder up reduces the lateral fragment.

Steps

StepDetail
Skin incisionAn oblique 8–10 cm incision just superior over the clavicle, centred over the fracture site. This incision works for fractures of the medial third.
DissectionCreate subcutaneous flaps anteriorly and posteriorly. At the medial end of the incision the sensory branches of the supraclavicular nerve may be encountered — identify and protect them. If damaged or sacrificed this leaves a small area of numbness inferior to the incision which patients tolerate well if warned preoperatively; however the cut cutaneous nerve can form a painful neuroma, so the supraclavicular nerve should not be sacrificed.
Deep exposureIncise the clavipectoral fascia to expose the fracture. Laterally a small area of pectoralis major attachment may require reflection at the fracture site — most attachment is left undisturbed. The deltoid must be reflected from the lateral clavicle anteriorly and posteriorly in a contiguous sheet.
Soft tissue preservationPreserve soft tissue attachments to all bone fragments to enable healing. Comminution is common; accurate reduction matters, but not at the expense of complete stripping. It is preferable to maintain fragment viability at the expense of some malreduction.
ClosureAfter copious irrigation, close the fascia and subcutaneous tissues in layers. Oppose the platysma layers exactly as previously cut so no skin deformity occurs. Close the clavipectoral fascia to cover the underlying plate and optimise healing. Pearl: incorporating the cut and elevated underlying periosteum with the fascia repair reduces dehiscence and strengthens the closure. Oppose the skin with great care and avoid tension for minimal scarring.

AO hook plate — reduction and fixation

AO Surgery Reference — LCP clavicle hook plate
Step 1 of 6
Indication
Hook plate fixation is indicated for selected cases of acute complete acromioclavicular joint dislocation and for reconstruction of chronic symptomatic acromioclavicular instability. Unlike many other methods, the hook plate does not rely on coracoid integrity, making it attractive when the coracoid is compromised. One drawback: following healing, plate removal is generally required to optimise range of motion and eliminate residual hardware discomfort.
Step 2 of 6
Hook placement and plate selection
Make a small incision at the posterior aspect of the AC joint to allow sub-acromial placement of the hook. Place the hook portion of the trial plate in the subacromial space at the posterior joint, then use the shaft portion to lever the clavicle into place. Use trial and error with the three different trial hook depths to determine optimal depth. Typically the short four-hole hook plate is adequate for most AC joint dislocations.
Step 3 of 6
Pitfall — hook depth
Too great a hook depth results in under-reduction, or residual superior displacement of the clavicle. Too small a hook depth over-reduces the clavicle, displacing it inferiorly and exerting excessive pressure on the acromion through the hook — acromial erosion or fracture can occur. When hook plate mechanical failure occurs, over-reduction is the most common contributing mechanism.
Step 4 of 6
Avoiding over-reduction
AO lists five intraoperative manoeuvres: (1) select a hook depth appropriate for the individual case; (2) contour the shaft or hook with hand-held bending irons, but avoid repeated bending which risks material failure; (3) avoid excessive downward pressure on the clavicle; (4) resect a superior bony prominence of the distal clavicle to give a flat surface for plate placement; (5) use intraoperative imaging with the trial in place when reduction is uncertain.
Step 5 of 6
Definitive fixation
Place the hook posteriorly under the acromion — correct posterior placement aids reduction and avoids rotator cuff impingement. The hook resists downward displacement of the arm through its subacromial position. To avoid excessive stress on any screw, insert the screw closest to the fracture first and tighten until appropriate resistance is felt; this may leave the plate proud, but sequential insertion of the following screws approximates it to the clavicle. This manoeuvre is only possible with regular screws — locking screws are contraindicated for it.
Step 6 of 6
Repair and check
If feasible, repair the coracoclavicular and AC ligaments with sutures. At the conclusion of fixation, carefully check the joint, plate and screws for accurate reduction, correct plate placement, and absence of intra-articular screw placement. If any doubt remains, take an intraoperative radiograph for confirmation.

Anatomic CC ligament reconstruction

Reconstruct both CC ligaments by fixing a tendon graft in two clavicle tunnels at the anatomic conoid and trapezoid insertions, with the remaining limb reconstructing the AC ligaments. Hook plate fixation is added for stability while the reconstruction heals and the graft matures.

Preoperative planning checklist

Table: arm holder or padded Mayo stand. Position: beach-chair with the hip flexed 60–70°; towel bump. Equipment: hook plate set with locking and nonlocking screws, flat braided high-tensile nonabsorbable suture (if not using hook plate fixation), Hewson suture passer, tendon harvester.

R&G 10e — authors' preferred technique for chronic symptomatic AC injury
Step 1 of 10
Positioning
Beach-chair position with the hip flexed 60–70°, positioned far lateral on the table to allow the arm to fall into extension. A small towel bump along the medial scapular border prevents scapular protraction and elevates the torso for tunnel drilling. Gently rotate and extend the head away from the operative field — but beware tension across the brachial plexus. Drape widely: from the SC joint to the nipple line, up the neck to the base of the ear, and several inches behind the posterior clavicle.
Step 2 of 10
Incision and deltotrapezial flaps
An oblique 'saber cut' incision over the lateral clavicle, extending toward the coracoid. Raise generous skin flaps directly above the fascia. Elevate the deltotrapezial fascia from the distal clavicle as full-thickness flaps, incising along the natural demarcation between trapezius (posterior) and deltoid (anterior). Dissect far enough medially to expose the conoid insertion, approximately 46 ± 5 mm from the distal clavicle. Place tagging stitches to aid retraction and accurate reapproximation at closure.
Step 3 of 10
Expose the coracoid
Split the deltoid vertically and expose the medial and lateral coracoid with dissection directly on bone. Pass a shuttling suture around the coracoid with a Lauer clamp with or without a Hewson suture passer, medial to lateral. This is a critical step — stay directly on bone to avoid entrapment or injury to the brachial plexus and axillary vessels.
Step 4 of 10
Drill the clavicle tunnels
Conoid guide pin: 45 mm medial to the distal clavicle, posterior to the clavicular midline in the coronal plane — err slightly more medial for better bone density. Trapezoid pin: 15 mm lateral to the conoid pin, just anterior to the midline, and not less than 25 mm from the clavicle end. Keep tunnels at least 3 mm from the clavicle edge toward the midline to avoid blowout. Protect underlying structures with a Cobb elevator. Use a 'ream-in, pull-out' technique so the tunnel is not eccentric; do not pass the far cortex.
Step 5 of 10
Prepare and pass the graft
Semitendinosus autograft is preferred; anterior tibialis allograft must be trimmed as it is often thick. Minimum length needed is about 110 mm with an ideal width of at least 5 mm. Prepare with a continuous running locked stitch of high-tensile nonabsorbable suture, pulled tight to tubularise the flat end. Pass beneath the coracoid on the shuttling suture, cross the limbs in figure-of-eight fashion, then shuttle through the bone tunnels inferior to superior, beginning with the conoid (posteromedial) tunnel.
Step 6 of 10
Reduce and fix
Reduce by elevating the scapulohumeral complex to the clavicle with an assistant pushing on the elbow — anatomical reduction is critical. Leave a short limb of approximately 2 cm exiting the conoid tunnel; the longer limb exits the trapezoid tunnel for later AC ligament reconstruction. Fix with 5.5 × 8 mm PEEK interference screws in the anterior aspect of each tunnel, conoid first, with the graft under tension. Tap the tunnels beforehand — this minimises graft creep and lowers torque and stress on the tunnel. PEEK has higher pull-out strength than bioabsorbable screws without cutting the tissue as metal can.
Step 7 of 10
Reconstruct the AC ligaments
Take the long graft limb lateral and posterior to augment the posterior capsule repair, incorporating it into the trapezius fascia; carry the remnant superiorly to augment the superior AC capsule repair with high-strength nonabsorbable suture. Suture the short conoid limb to the base of the long trapezoid limb to create a closed figure-of-eight loop. Repair AC capsule remnants with figure-of-eight absorbable stitches.
Step 8 of 10
Apply the hook plate
Trial hook depth before choosing the definitive plate — too shallow causes over-reduction. Account for the graft thickness that will sit beneath the plate: select a depth approximately +2 mm larger. Contour the hook with bending irons to match the acromial undersurface and avoid point loading. Choose a plate length that bypasses the bone tunnels, and place screws medial to the tunnels. Ensure the hook is fully seated beneath the acromion.
Step 9 of 10
Closure
Deltotrapezial fascia closure is an essential step — it adds strength and blood supply to the reconstruction. Close the large flaps tightly with interrupted high-strength nonabsorbable sutures using a 'pants-over-vest' technique, with knots tied on the inferior side to minimise skin irritation. Deep dermis with buried 3-0 Vicryl, skin with a running subcuticular stitch. Obtain radiographs in recovery to quantify reduction, tunnel and plate position.
Step 10 of 10
Postoperative care
Sling or abduction brace for 4–6 weeks, removed for hygiene and gentle pendulum exercises. Strengthening at 6–12 weeks if pain-free normal ROM, targeting scapular stabilisers that retract the scapula and decrease AC loads. Weight training at 3 months. Full-contact athletics at 6 months, though 9–12 months is generally needed to regain peak strength. Remove the hook plate at 9–12 months to decrease acromial osteolysis and hardware pain; then refrain from contact activity for 6–8 weeks to allow screw holes to consolidate.
Surgical pitfalls and preventions — AC
PitfallPrevention
Bunching of graft tissue preventing complete reductionDo not cross the graft around the neck of the coracoid; leave as a single loop.
Clavicle fracture or bone tunnel wideningAvoid drilling tunnels >5.5 mm. Tap the clavicle tunnels before interference screw insertion. Ensure an adequate bridge of bone between tunnels.
Loss of reductionEnsure the patient is compliant with postoperative rehabilitation; use of a hook plate generally prevents this.
Not contouring the hook plateContour the hook to the undersurface of the acromion.
Over-reduction of the AC jointTrial the various depths of hook plate before choosing the definitive size.
Leaving the hook plate in too longPlan a scheduled hardware removal at 9–12 months.

SC joint — open repair and reconstruction

The fundamental objective is stabilisation of the medial clavicle to an adjacent structure, regardless of the initial direction of displacement — so the same techniques serve anterior and posterior instability.

Two decisions

DECISION ONE
Which tissue
Local ligaments and capsule, tendon transfer of subclavius or sternocleidomastoid, or a free graft.
DECISION TWO
Stabilise to what
The first rib, the manubrium, or both.
BIOMECHANICS
Figure-of-eight wins
Spencer et al.: semitendinosus figure-of-eight had superior initial mechanical properties to intramedullary ligament repair and subclavius transfer.
NEVER
K-wires and pins
Largely historical due to high complication rates, especially pin migration — a recent review states this is absolutely contraindicated.

Further principles

  • Minimise disruption of the anterior ligament structures as much as possible. Resection of the medial clavicle is rarely recommended as it tends to exacerbate instability.
  • Kendal et al. review of 108 cases found five procedures most commonly performed: tendon graft ligament reconstruction; local soft tissue repair or synthetic reconstruction; medial clavicular resection with or without ligament transfer; ORIF; and tendon transfer techniques.
  • Outcomes are significantly better for acute than chronic dislocations — accurate diagnosis and prompt treatment as close to the time of injury as possible is optimal.
  • Vertigan et al. type series: 86% return to sport and 96% survivorship at mean 94.5 months with figure-of-eight reconstruction. Kusnezov et al. reported worse results in a military population — 35.7% complications, 14.3% recurrent instability.
R&G 10e — acute transosseous repair, medial clavicle resection, figure-of-eight graft
Step 1 of 8
Position and approach
Supine on a radiolucent table with the chest, abdomen and ipsilateral limb prepped and draped free — drape the entire chest for posterior dislocations in the rare event vascular injury requires sternotomy. Make a curvilinear incision over the SC joint with the horizontal limb in line with the clavicle and the vertical limb along the manubrium. Elevate skin flaps and incise the periosteum horizontally, taking care to preserve the capsule for later repair.
Step 2 of 8
Reduction and capsular repair
Reduce the posteriorly displaced clavicle with traction, towel-clip elevation, and/or by gently leveraging it from posterior to anterior with a blunt retractor. Incorporate the posterior capsule together with the intra-articular disc ligament into a running locking no. 2 Ethibond suture. Pass drill holes through the clavicle from anterior to posterior, protecting the neurovascular structures, and shuttle the sutures through the posterior cortex with a Hewson passer.
Step 3 of 8
Complete the transosseous repair
Repair the posterior capsular defect with interrupted permanent suture. After the defect is closed, secure the previously passed transosseous sutures along the anterior cortex. Close the remaining capsular sleeve with absorbable sutures to complete the repair.
Step 4 of 8
Medial clavicle resection (Rockwood & Wirth)
Indicated for severely damaged medial articulations, to decompress posterior structures, or to give the thoracic surgeon access to the mediastinum. Preserve the anterior capsular ligament during exposure. If the costoclavicular ligaments are intact, resect the clavicle medial to the ligaments and bevel it smooth; if torn, the clavicle must be stabilised to the first rib. Limit resection to 10 mm or less for degenerative change (Bisson et al.: safe resection 1 cm in men, 0.9 cm in women). If the anterior capsule is insufficient, resect the medial 2.5–3.5 cm and secure the residual clavicle to the first rib with 1-mm Dacron tape. Protect vascular structures with a Crego elevator or ribbon retractor behind the medial clavicle during resection.
Step 5 of 8
Intramedullary ligament transfer
Drill and curette the medullary canal of the medial clavicle to receive the transferred intra-articular disc ligament. Place two small drill holes in the superior cortex approximately 1 cm lateral to the resection, communicating with the canal. Pass the suture ends into the canal and out through these holes; with the clavicle held reduced to the first rib and sternum, pull the ligament tightly into the canal and tie over the cortical bone bridge. Complete with five or six 1-mm Dacron sutures around the periosteal tube, clavicle, residual costoclavicular ligament and first-rib periosteum — the aim is to restore the normal clavicle–rib space, not to pull it tight, which would reduce the space and cause pain.
Step 6 of 8
Figure-of-eight tendon graft
The authors' preferred reconstruction when acute repair is not possible due to late presentation or poor tissue quality. Expose the SC joint as for acute repair, preserving the periosteal sleeve. Create drill holes in both the clavicle and the manubrium, passed from anterior to posterior. Weave a free semitendinosus graft through the holes so the strands lie parallel posterior to the joint and cross anterior to it. Spencer et al. showed this figure-of-eight construct has superior initial mechanical properties to intramedullary ligament repair and subclavius tendon transfer.
Step 7 of 8
Tension and secure
Reduce the SC joint and pass the tendon graft through the bone tunnels with a suture passer. Prepare the graft with a running locking permanent suture to reinforce it and prevent fraying. Tension the graft, tie the ends in a square knot and secure with multiple no. 2 Ethibond sutures.
Step 8 of 8
Postoperative care
If open reduction was required, a sling is used for 6 weeks. Avoid pushing, pulling or lifting; the involved arm may be used for bodily needs — eating, drinking, dressing, toilet care. After 12 weeks the patient gradually resumes usual daily living activities, including overhead activity. After medial clavicle resection with first-rib stabilisation, hold the shoulders back in a figure-of-eight dressing for 4–6 weeks.
Table 32-2 — surgical techniques for sternoclavicular reconstruction
ProcedureTechnique
Open excision with intramedullary ligament repairUse the intra-articular disc ligament as a transfer into the medial clavicle, reinforced with local tissue repair.
Soft tissue graft, figure-of-eightReconstitute the capsular ligaments with graft — described with semitendinosus or plantaris tendon graft.
Subclavius tenodesis (Burrows)Use a slip of subclavius to reconstruct the costoclavicular ligament; modification uses fascia lata graft.
Sternocleidomastoid to first rib and claviclePartial SCM slip through the first rib and clavicle to recreate the costoclavicular ligament.
Sternocleidomastoid to clavicle and manubriumPartial SCM slip to recreate the capsular ligaments, with no exposure of the first rib.
Plate stabilisationBalser (hook) plate inserted behind or into the manubrium with local capsule repair — removal required. Ledge plate: standard 3.5 mm LC/DCP six-hole plate placed anteriorly with the medial two holes over the manubrium. Locking plate: two 3.5 mm precontoured locking plates at 90° to each other.
Surgical pitfalls and preventions — SC
PitfallPrevention
Neurovascular or cardiopulmonary events; thorax perforation with possible pneumo- or haemothoraxAlways get a chest x-ray after surgical treatment.
Hardware issues; prominent hardware needing removalMedial clavicle anatomy is difficult for plate positioning — minifragment plates may work better, and bone fixation may be less secure than laterally.

AO aftercare — four phases

PhaseDetail
Phase 1 — week 1–3 (inflammatory)Principle: protection of the injured limb to facilitate uneventful healing. Aim: healing without complications while facilitating early movement. Full-time external support: optimal shoulder immobilisation secures the upper arm and forearm to the chest — a sling supporting the elbow and forearm, with a swathe around the humerus and chest. For coracoid or acromial fractures and rotator cuff surgery, an abduction cushion or airplane splint relieves tension by elevation and abduction. Mobilise unaffected joints (hand, wrist, elbow, neck, scapular squeezes) to reduce swelling and preserve proprioception. Active-assisted ROM with gravity eliminated: external and internal rotation at waist level, forward flexion without scapular protraction with the forearm supported. Isometric cuff and deltoid strengthening as comfort permits. ADLs limited to personal care; sleep in the sling on the back or non-injured side.
Phase 2 — week 4–6 (early repair)Principle: continued protection with promotion of directed tissue repair. Aim: established healing with antigravity strength. Sling and abduction brace at night and for all activities under gravity, weaning to part-time. Actively assisted elevation to shoulder level introduced. Avoid hand behind back and extreme across-body adduction at this stage — this avoids adverse rotation of the clavicle and scapula. Tabletop-level domestic activity encouraged. Radiographic union expected; confirmation with symptom reduction permits progression.
Phase 3 — week 7–12 (late repair, early remodeling)Principle: reestablishment of proprioception. Aim: normal tissue structure and reinnervation through daily activity without secondary injury. Wean from full-time support. Actively assisted elevation above shoulder level introduced. Hand behind back and across-body adduction are now permitted — these facilitate rotation of the clavicle and scapula. Isometric and isokinetic strengthening of cuff, deltoid and periscapular muscles permitted. Exercise bar, rope and pulley, therabands, progressing to resistance machines and free weights. Radiographic consolidation expected.
Phase 4 — week 13 onward (remodeling and reintegration)Principle: normalisation of proprioceptive function with optimal biomechanics. Aim: normal tissue structure and reinnervation through training and practice for optimal endurance. Sport or occupational work-hardening exercises introduced under supervision, with no limits of movement. All activities including sport and occupational tasks requiring resisted elevation and abduction are encouraged.

Common adverse outcomes

  • Loss of reduction, small visual deformity on x-rays
  • Clavicle fracture at bone tunnels
  • Infection or soft tissue envelope healing
  • AC arthritis or AC joint pain with residual posterior instability
  • Hardware or implant pain requiring removal
  • Cosmetic bumps or late degenerative changes

Complications of AC joint surgery

Loss of reduction

Reported at 10–30%, varying largely due to inconsistent radiographic grading.

  • In high-grade dislocation the weight of the entire upper extremity is supported through a limited area of fixation, producing complex loading.
  • Prudent follow-up and rehabilitation compliance are essential.
  • In the authors' experience, well-executed hook plate fixation is the most reliable method to avoid this.

Hardware failure

Limited use of K-wires, pins and Bosworth screws should considerably reduce hardware complications and pin migration, but newer suture buttons, tightropes and hook plates can still fail.

  • Technical errors to avoid: over-reduction from too shallow a hook (measure distal clavicle thickness on preoperative x-rays to guide depth); inadequate hook contouring causing point loading on the acromion; and inadequate medial screw fixation leading to plate pull-off.
  • Failure of modern implants is concerning for infection and should be investigated as such.

Acromial erosion and osteolysis

Hook plates require removal in most patients because of significant risk of acromial osteolysis and erosion over time.

  • Over-reduction from an incorrect hook depth and inadequate contouring drives the hook through the acromion.
  • Plates can also be prominent and cause soft tissue discomfort.

Coracoid fracture

Clavicle fracture is a real intraoperative complication — bone tunnels must be smaller than 5.5 mm with adequate bone between the hole and the posteroanterior cortex to avoid a stress riser. Coracoid base fracture is a described mode of failure for cortical button suspensory fixation.

Failure of soft tissue repairs

Simple repair of the CC and AC ligaments without additional support of CC sutures, screws or internal fixation will likely fail — particularly in chronic injury where displacement between clavicle and coracoid is significant.

  • Weaver–Dunn transfer alone is generally not strong enough and must be supplemented.
  • Early failure usually warrants reoperation; failure weeks to months later should raise suspicion of infection.

Graft erosion, foreign body reaction, infection

CC fixation with grafts or synthetic material has been associated with various complications. Neault et al. reported three cases where nonabsorbable tape or suture was directly related to postoperative infection — two within a year, but one occurring 5 years after repair of a type III injury.

Acromioclavicular arthritis

May occur after surgical fixation; the distal 8–10 mm of clavicle can be excised if this is a concern.

  • There is no consensus on primary distal clavicle excision for acute AC injuries.
  • The authors preserve the AC articulation whenever possible, but remove scar within the dislocation space including the meniscus homolog to allow reduction.
  • If any distal clavicle is removed, they take it from the posterior edge — the typical site of abutment or impingement with the posterior acromion.

Anatomy is the prevention

MISTAKE ONE
Inadequate exposure
Failing to expose the AC joint fully, and failing to remove calcified tissue or scar within the CC space, prevents anatomic reduction.
MISTAKE TWO
Tunnels too large
Keep bone tunnels under 5.5 mm, with adequate bone between the hole and the posteroanterior cortex.
MISTAKE THREE
Fascia left open
Closure of the deltotrapezial fascia is essential — it adds strength and blood supply to the repair.
MISTAKE FOUR
Untrialled hook
Trial the available sizes and contour the blade to the acromial undersurface to prevent point loading and impingement.
MISTAKE FIVE
Plate left in
Careful postoperative monitoring ensures removal before significant acromial osteolysis occurs.

Complications of SC joint injury

ANTERIOR
Essentially cosmetic
Nonoperative complications are limited to cosmetic bumps or late degenerative changes, though some patients report pain and discomfort.
POSTERIOR
Where the danger is
Serious complications at the time of dislocation are primarily limited to posterior injuries.
WORMAN & LEAGUS
16 of 60 (26.7%)
Patients reviewed from the literature suffered complications of the trachea, oesophagus or great vessels.
AFTER SURGERY
15.6% complications
Recurrence rare at 4%. Implant removal in up to 80% of revision cases. Failure to return to sport in 25%, usually from mobility restriction.

Reported sequelae of retrosternal dislocation

  • Right pulmonary artery laceration
  • Transected internal mammary artery with lacerated brachiocephalic vein
  • Pneumothorax with laceration of the superior vena cava
  • Tracheal stenosis and respiratory distress
  • Venous congestion in the neck
  • Oesophageal rupture with abscess and clavicular osteomyelitis
  • Pressure on and late occlusion of the subclavian artery in untreated patients
  • Subclavian vein obstruction from an unreduced Salter–Harris II medial physeal injury
  • Compression and thrombosis of the brachiocephalic vein
  • Myocardial conduction abnormalities
  • Compression of the right common carotid artery
  • Pseudoaneurysm of the right subclavian artery
  • Brachial plexus compression
  • Hoarseness, onset of snoring, voice change to falsetto with arm movement
  • Fatal tracheoesophageal fistula
  • Mediastinal compression
  • Severe thoracic outlet syndrome with swelling and cyanosis

Annotated references

StudyAnnotation
Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society (2015)RCT of nonoperative sling vs hook plate fixation for acute type III–V AC injuries in 83 patients. Hook plate gave superior radiographic alignment but was not clinically superior. The nonoperative group had better early functional outcomes; both improved to good or excellent at 2 years. Level I.
Murray IR et al. — ACORN (2018)RCT of nonoperative sling vs tightrope tunnelled suspensory device in 60 patients with acute grade III–IV dislocations. Nonoperative recovered faster with no benefit of surgery at 1 year; 5 patients crossed over. Level I.
Joukainen A et al. (2014)Prospective randomised trial of type III and V at 18–20 years — the longest follow-up in the literature. No significant difference in functional outcome; nonoperative group had more prominent and wider AC joints. Level III.
Verstift DE et al. (2021)Longest follow-up of nonoperatively treated type I and II at 8–10 years: no significant functional impairment or arthritis versus the normal contralateral side. Level III.
Fukuda K et al. (1986)Biomechanical study of the AC ligamentous system — key anatomic distances and the effect of sequential sectioning on stability. Commonly tested on examinations.
Williams GR, Nguyen VD, Rockwood CR (1989)Landmark paper describing the classification of AC joint injuries — one of the few classification systems that helps guide treatment.
Tauber M et al. (2009)Prospective comparison of modified Weaver–Dunn vs semitendinosus autograft for chronic AC dislocation. Superior clinical and radiologic outcomes in the semitendinosus group. 24 patients, Level II.
Gowd AK et al. (2019)Most up-to-date systematic review and meta-analysis of modern operative techniques. Significant complication profiles exist in most techniques; no difference between open and arthroscopic on complication incidence.
Kendal JK et al. (2018)Systematic review of posterior SC dislocation outcomes. Good overall outcomes with 16% complication rate. Closed reduction should be attempted within 48 hours, reduction confirmed on axial CT; unsuccessful closed reduction should prompt open reduction.
Sernandez H, Riehl J (2019)Systematic review of 92 patients — closed reduction should be attempted in all traumatic dislocations. If unsuccessful, open reduction should be performed rather than leaving the joint dislocated, which led to poor outcomes in up to 42%.
Leonard DA et al. (2020)National sample showing 0% incidence of vascular injuries with posterior SC dislocations — challenging the dogma of requiring cardiothoracic backup. Level III.
Boesmueller S et al. (2016)92 SC injuries at median 11 years: good to excellent outcome in up to 93%. Chronic injuries slightly worse; paediatric injuries nearly universally excellent.
